newsitem.title: INDIA: India quake's depth made it less deadly - expert.
newsitem.headline: India quake's depth made it less deadly - expert.

text.p: A powerful earthquake that killed dozens of people in central India on Thursday reminded many of a quake in 1993 that left about 10,000 dead.

But the 1993 quake, which struck the Latur-Osmanabad region of the state of Maharashtra, was deadlier in part because it originated much closer to the earth's surface than the tremor in Madhya Pradesh state on Thursday, a seismology department official in the capital New Delhi said.

"The depth of the earthquake in Latur was only about six km (four miles)," seismologist S.N. Bhattacharya told Reuters. "But the focus of today's earthquake lay about 30 km (20 miles) below the epicentre."
The Latur quake measured 6.3 on the Richter scale, while Thursday's measured 6.0. Both caused widespread devastation.
The epicentre of Thursday's quake lay in Kosamghat, a village in the Narmada River basin in central India.
As rescue teams dug through the debris of flattened houses, officials said at least 35 people were confirmed dead, as many as 1,000 injured and at least as many left homeless.
Authorities said they expected to find more bodies but that they did not anticipate a sharp rise in the death toll.
"The soil in the Narmada river basin is solid and strong, while in Latur it was loose, eroded soil," Bhattacharya said. "The acceleration and the impact of the quake depends on the soil also."
Bhattacharya said the houses in Latur were badly designed, with fragile roofs and walls, while the houses in Madhya Pradesh were sturdier and built on firmer soil.
"But the Narmada region is more susceptible to earthquakes because it lies along two fault lines which are very active," he said.
The Narmada area has been rocked by five earthquakes measuring at least 5.5 on the Richter scale since 1927, the seismologist said.
